summaries.example: Imagine a student asking, “If people are guided by God, can they still choose what to do?” Ibn Daud thought careful thinking could help explain how religious teachings and human choice fit together. He also believed that learning and good actions help a person become wiser and better.
summaries.summary: Abraham Ibn Daud was a Jewish philosopher of the twelfth century. His main philosophical book, The Exalted Faith, was written to defend Judaism while using ideas from Aristotle and Muslim thinkers. Ibn Daud wanted to help readers understand how Scripture and reason could agree, especially about free will. He arranged his book like a guided course: first he explained nature, matter, motion, the soul, and other philosophical topics; then he discussed God, angels, prophecy, and human choice; finally he wrote about ethics and religious practice. He held that knowledge and good actions lead people toward perfection. His work was important because it brought Aristotelian philosophy into Jewish thought in a systematic way. Later, Maimonides wrote a more famous philosophical work, and Ibn Daud’s book became less widely used, although it continued to influence later thinkers. The SEP entry also notes that some parts of Ibn Daud’s system remain unclear, including how creation and the activity of heavenly intelligences fit together.
key_ideas: Abraham Ibn Daud was a Jewish philosopher who lived in medieval Spain and Toledo.
His book The Exalted Faith tried to show that philosophy and Jewish religious teaching could work together.
He used ideas from Aristotle and Muslim philosophers, especially Al-Farabi and Ibn Sina.
He argued that people can choose between good and evil, though his explanation has difficult questions.
He connected knowledge, good character, justice, and religious practice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ibn Daud’s work shows how a thinker can bring ideas from different intellectual traditions into conversation. It also raises a lasting question: how can people explain religious teachings while taking reason seriously? His book matters in the history of Jewish philosophy because it helped establish a systematic Aristotelian approach before Maimonides.

important_terms.definition: A person’s ability to think, understand, and use reasons.
The ability to choose between different actions.
The part of a thing that makes it what it is.
A way of thinking about nature, knowledge, and what is real.

questions_to_think_about: Can careful thinking and religious belief help each other?
What makes a choice genuinely free?
Can learning help someone become a better person?
Why might a writer use ideas from other cultures to explain their own tradition?

summaries.example: Consider the question of whether a person’s action is free if God already knows what will happen. Ibn Daud’s distinctive answer is that God does not foreknow human choices in the same way that God knows necessary events. Human choices belong to a special class of causes: they can turn out in more than one way. Once a person chooses, the intelligences assist in carrying out that choice. This view protects freedom, but the SEP notes that it creates serious problems about divine knowledge and whether later repentance is possible.
summaries.summary: Abraham Ibn Daud was a twelfth-century Jewish philosopher associated with Muslim Spain and Toledo. His principal philosophical work, The Exalted Faith, sought to defend rabbinic Judaism through Aristotelian reasoning as transmitted by Muslim philosophers, especially Al-Farabi and Ibn Sina. Ibn Daud begins with logic, substance, matter, form, motion, infinity, and the soul. He then applies this preparation to religious principles: God’s existence and unity, divine attributes, heavenly intelligences, prophecy, Mosaic Law, and free will. The final part turns to ethics and religious practice. This order is significant: intellectual inquiry is presented as preparation for a good life rather than as an end detached from conduct. Ibn Daud’s account of God uses two kinds of argument. One begins from motion and concludes to a first unmoved mover; another begins from contingent beings and concludes to a Necessary Being. He identifies this philosophical first principle with the biblical God, although the entry notes that the identification is not fully argued. God’s absolute unity also leads Ibn Daud to interpret divine predicates as negations or relations. In his psychology, the rational soul can attain an acquired intellect and survive separation from the body. His account of freedom distinguishes genuine possibilities from matters that seem possible only because of human ignorance. Human moral choices belong to the former category, so God does not foreknow them as fixed outcomes. This defense of freedom is unusual in Jewish philosophy, but it leaves tensions concerning divine knowledge, the intellect’s role in choice, evil, and repentance. key_ideas: Ibn Daud’s Exalted Faith is the first systematic attempt to introduce the Aristotelianism of Muslim philosophers into Jewish philosophy.
He presents philosophy as a tool for interpreting difficult biblical passages and seeking harmony between reason and revelation.
The book moves from Aristotelian physics and metaphysics to God, intelligences, prophecy, free choice, ethics, and religious practice.
His arguments for God’s existence appeal to motion and to the difference between necessary and contingent beings rather than beginning from creation.
He treats the soul as an incorporeal substance whose rational capacity can become perfected through knowledge and correct action.

His account of free will limits divine foreknowledge of human actions, yet the overall system contains unresolved tensions, including the status of matter and the relation between emanation and creation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ibn Daud is important both historically and philosophically. Historically, he helped create a sustained Jewish Aristotelianism by adapting arguments and concepts from Arabic philosophy to Jewish concerns. Philosophically, he illustrates the difficulty of building one system from revelation, metaphysics, psychology, and ethics. His unresolved questions—especially about divine knowledge, matter, creation, and emanation—show that philosophical influence does not require a system to be complete or free of tension.

important_terms.definition: The basic reality or essence of a thing; in Ibn Daud’s Aristotelian framework, it is contrasted with an attribute that exists in something else.
A feature that belongs to a thing but does not constitute its essence, such as a changeable quality or relation.
A being whose essence is sufficient for its existence and which does not depend on another cause.
The view that human choices are not fixed in advance and can be directed toward contrary alternatives.
The incorporeal intellect that, in Ibn Daud’s account, helps move human understanding from possibility to achieved knowledge.
A claim about God that avoids treating divine qualities as parts of God’s essence; Ibn Daud often interprets such claims negatively or relationally.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining difficult scriptural passages philosophically preserve their religious meaning, or change it?
Is limiting divine foreknowledge a convincing way to defend human freedom?
How might Ibn Daud’s account of divine attributes avoid making God internally multiple?
Why does a philosophical system need a transition from theoretical knowledge to ethical and religious practice?
What should we conclude when a thinker’s central argument solves one contradiction but creates new problems?

summaries.example: Suppose your school has a rule that says students are responsible for their choices, but someone asks whether every choice was already fixed. Ibn Daud would say that some events are necessary, while human choices can genuinely go in either of two directions. A person may choose to act fairly or unfairly. Knowledge and religious practice can help the person choose well, but the choice is still theirs.
summaries.summary: Abraham Ibn Daud was a Jewish philosopher who lived during the twelfth century, first in Muslim Spain and later in Toledo. His major philosophical work, The Exalted Faith, was written to defend Judaism by using a carefully organized form of Aristotelian philosophy. Ibn Daud believed that reason and Scripture should not be enemies. People have intellects, he argued, so they should use them to understand difficult religious questions. His book begins with subjects that prepare a student for theology: logic, substance and accident, matter and form, motion, infinity, and the soul. It then turns to religious principles, including God’s existence and unity, divine attributes, heavenly intelligences, prophecy, and free will. Its last section discusses ethics and religious practice. Ibn Daud’s account of God draws on arguments from motion and from the idea of a Necessary Being. He explains the soul as a nonphysical substance with different powers, the highest being the rational or speculative power. This power links human beings with intelligences and God through knowledge. Ibn Daud’s discussion of free will comes near the end because it depends on the earlier discussions. He says that some things are necessary, while others are genuinely open to opposite outcomes. Human moral actions belong to this second group. He therefore limits divine foreknowledge of human choices in order to protect freedom. His theory is inventive but difficult: the entry points to tensions involving evil, the role of intellect in choice, repentance, and the unclear relationship between creation and emanation. The work was later overshadowed by Maimonides, but its influence continued in medieval Jewish philosophy.
key_ideas: Ibn Daud wrote in the twelfth century and became an early major Jewish Aristotelian thinker.
His philosophical book The Exalted Faith aimed to defend Judaism by combining Jewish learning with ideas from Aristotle and Muslim philosophers.
He thought philosophy could help interpret biblical passages that seem to disagree, especially passages about human freedom.
His book teaches basic philosophy first, then discusses God, prophecy, angels or intelligences, free will, ethics, and religious practice.
He believed the soul’s highest power is its ability to understand, and that knowledge and good action help a person reach perfection.
The entry presents his system as influential but not completely settled: some explanations, such as the origin of matter, remain unclear.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ibn Daud’s work helps us see medieval philosophy as a meeting place for Jewish, Greek, and Muslim intellectual traditions. It also shows that questions about freedom, knowledge, God, and moral responsibility are connected. His attempt to make philosophy support religious life influenced later Jewish thinkers, even though his answers were not always complete or consistent.

important_terms.definition: Using careful thinking and reasons to understand a question.
The power to select among possible actions, including different moral choices.
The basic kind of thing something is, rather than a feature it happens to have.
A changeable feature of a thing that is not its basic essence.
A being that depends on nothing else for its existence; Ibn Daud uses this idea in an argument for God.
Nonphysical heavenly beings that connect the divine and earthly realms in Ibn Daud’s philosophical picture.

questions_to_think_about: When should a difficult religious passage be read literally, and when might it need interpretation?
Can a person be responsible for an action if that action is completely determined?
Why might Ibn Daud place lessons about nature and the soul before lessons about God and religion?
Does becoming knowledgeable automatically make someone morally better?
What can later philosophers gain from a work that contains unanswered questions?
